॥ Om, the wordless (ashabda) of the Seer (Iksate) ॥ 1/1/5 ॥

One might object: “Is it not the case that the object of contemplation is beyond the reach of words and mind, as stated in the verses: ‘From which words turn back, unable to reach it, together with the mind’; ‘That which is wordless, touchless, formless, imperishable, tasteless, eternal, and odorless’; ‘It is spoken of only by the wordless’; ‘That which words do not express, by which words are expressed’; ‘That which the ear does not hear, by which this ear hears’?” Therefore, it is not within the scope of words.

In response, it is stated: “The wordless (ashabda) of the Seer (Iksate).” It is indeed expressible (vacya) because it is the object of contemplation (iksaniya), as indicated by statements such as: “He contemplates the Supreme Person, the Lord of the Self, who is beyond this dense mass of living beings and beyond the beyond”; “One should see the Self in the Self”; and “Having known, one should cultivate wisdom.” It is not to be contemplated by the wordless (anavacana) because it is Upanishadic in nature. This is also supported by the Shrutis and Smritis, as in: “All the Vedas speak of that word (padam); all the austerities speak of that”; and “I alone am to be known by all the Vedas; I am the creator of the Vedas and the knower of the Vedas.” The claim that it is inexpressible (avacya) and so on is not established (aprasiddha).

As it is said: “It is not to be known as such, nor spoken of, nor reasoned about. Even those who see do not see My form, O wise ones.”

And in the Garuda Purana: “It is inexpressible due to its non-establishment, yet it is expressible because it is declared by all the Agamas. It is not to be reasoned about, yet it is to be reasoned about; it is not to be known, yet it is to be known. Thus, the Supreme is remembered.”

Furthermore, the wordlessness (ashabdatta) of the object is not established by other means. ॥ 5 ॥
